# Breaking a big user story into small ones — the plain-English version

> **Who this is for:** me (FED lead) — the clear, low-jargon version I can actually retain.
> **What it's from:** Jas (our BA) asked how to split `SFCC-195`, the PDP "Product Information
> Accordion" (those expandable tabs on the product page). Tim's been pushing everyone to write
> smaller, "one-component-at-a-time" stories. This is what I took away.
> **The deal:** simplified, not dumbed down. Where I use a real name (Contentful, AP21…), I explain
> it in normal words the first time. Glossary at the bottom.

---

## The one thing to really get

Picture the accordion as a **filing cabinet**, and each tab as a **drawer**:

> Details & Care · Size & Fit · Shipping & Returns · Assistance · Environmental Qualities

Jas's first idea: **one ticket per drawer.** Feels tidy.

Here's the catch — **all the drawers look the same** (a label, and some text that opens up). The thing that's actually *different* is **where the paper inside each drawer comes from**:

- **Details & Care, Size & Fit** → from the **product record** (info stored on the product itself)
- **Shipping & Returns, Assistance** → from **Contentful** (the tool the content team edits without a developer)
- **Environmental Qualities** → from **AP21** (the product data system), EU shops only

So the smart cut isn't "one ticket per drawer." It's **"group the drawers by where their paper comes from."**

➡️ **The lesson in one line: split by where the content comes from, not by what the shopper sees.**

Why? Because the real work is building the *pipe* that fetches each kind of paper. Two drawers fed by the same pipe = the same work = one ticket. Splitting them into two tickets just means building the same pipe twice.

That took Jas's 6 tickets down to about 4, cut along the pipes instead of the drawers.

---

## Lesson 1 — a ticket should be something you can actually show

Jas's plan started with a "just the empty cabinet, no drawers" ticket. Problem: **you can't demo an empty cabinet.** Nobody can look at it and go "yep, that works."

Fix: **put one real drawer inside the cabinet ticket** so there's something to see and tick off.

➡️ Rule of thumb: every ticket should be a thin but *whole* strip — something a person can look at and sign off — never a hidden layer no one can see.

---

## Lesson 2 — we've done this before, so copy the pattern (don't invent one)

When Tim says "component-based stories," he's describing something the team **already did** on the filters work:
- one ticket to build the shared piece once,
- one ticket to plug it into each page.

(For the record: `SFCC-108` built the shared filter component, `SFCC-199` plugged it into the listing page. "Recently Viewed," `SFCC-83`, did the same.)

➡️ Lesson for me as lead: my proposals get an easy "yes" when I say *"this is the same shape as the filters work"* instead of inventing a new approach. Point at the last time we did it.

---

## Lesson 3 — split again when one drawer is riskier than another

Details & Care and Size & Fit both come from the product record — so by my own rule, that's one ticket. **But** Size & Fit needs a **new bit of product info that doesn't exist yet** (someone still has to confirm it with the business). Details & Care uses info we already have.

So I kept them apart. If I bundle them, the safe one gets stuck waiting on the unsure one.

➡️ Rule of thumb: same source = group them. But if one piece is **waiting on an unknown** (info not confirmed, content not written, a tool not built) — split it off so it doesn't drag the rest down.

---

## Lesson 4 — don't drag in something another team is building later; let it wait politely

The "Assistance" drawer *looked* like it might be special. It has email, phone, opening hours, WhatsApp, a contact link… and a **"Start a Chat"** button.

Everything except the chat button is just text and links — same as the Shipping & Returns drawer. The chat button is the only real difference, because it opens the **live chat widget**, and that widget:
- can't switch on until the shopper accepts cookies,
- decides its own "are we online right now" behaviour,
- and is being built by **another team, in a later sprint** — it doesn't exist yet.

We have a written rule: **don't build against something from a later sprint.**

So the move was: **build the drawer now, but make the chat button harmless until the widget shows up.** If the chat's there, the button opens it; if not, it just sits quietly. Wire it up properly later, when the other team's part lands.

➡️ End result: Assistance stayed in **one** ticket with Shipping & Returns, and the chat button became a small "come back to this later" note tied to the other team's work. Nothing got blocked.

(The proper name for "still works, just quietly does less, when a piece is missing" is *graceful degradation*. Worth knowing — it's often the trick that lets you keep one ticket instead of splitting or blocking.)

---

## Lesson 5 — if the ticket assumes something the spec hasn't decided, say so

The ticket confidently said "these drawers come from Contentful, those from the product record." But our actual spec (the PRD) **still lists that exact decision as "not decided yet."**

I flagged it — politely — because the whole split leans on that decision. If it changes later, the split falls apart.

➡️ Lesson: before I build a plan on a "fact," I check the spec. If the ticket is running ahead of the spec, I raise it instead of quietly assuming.

---

## Lesson 6 — talk to a BA in BA language

In my head this was all "fetch, sanitise, cookie-gate, degrade." What I actually **sent Jas** was: how many tickets, what's bundled, what's a dependency, which team/sprint owns what, and what keeps us unblocked.

I also said out loud where **her** idea was better (more tickets = easier to track progress and hand out to different people), so it felt like we decided together — not like I overruled her.

➡️ Lesson: do the deep thinking for myself; send the plain, scope-and-dependencies version to them. And always name the trade-offs of their idea — it builds trust and gets to "yes" faster.

---

## My quick checklist (steal this next time)

1. **Read everything first** — the ticket, the spec bit it points to, and check whether the thing even exists in our code yet.
2. For each part, ask **"where does its content come from?"** and group the parts that share a source.
3. **Split again** wherever one part is waiting on an unknown.
4. Make every ticket **demoable** — give the "shell" ticket one real drawer.
5. Anything **another team / later sprint owns** → don't pull it in; build it to sit quietly until their part lands.
6. **Point at the last time we split something the same way** — makes the "yes" easy.
7. If the ticket assumes something the spec hasn't settled, **flag it.**
8. Someone wants more tickets just for tracking? Use **sub-tasks**, not extra stories.
9. Write the reply in **their** language, and name where their idea wins.

---

## Words I used (so they stop being scary)

- **Vertical slice / walking skeleton** — a thin but *complete* piece you can actually show and tick off. Opposite: an invisible layer no one can see.
- **Data source** — where a piece of content actually comes from (our product system vs the content tool vs AP21).
- **Dependency** — something this work needs that lives elsewhere (another ticket, team, or sprint).
- **Graceful degradation** — building it so it still works, just quietly does less, when a piece it wants isn't ready yet.
- **Cookie-gated / consent-gated** — can't switch on until the shopper accepts cookies.
- **Contentful** — the content tool the marketing/content team edits without needing a developer.
- **AP21** — the product data system a lot of our product info comes from.
- **PRD** — the spec / "what we agreed to build" document. Source of truth for requirements.
- **Sprint / squad** — a sprint is a ~2-week chunk of work; a squad is one of our two teams. "Later sprint / other squad" = not our job right now.
- **Sub-task vs story** — a story is a standalone chunk of value; a sub-task is a checklist item *inside* a story. Use sub-tasks when you want finer tracking without more standalone tickets.

---

## Still to do
- Write the "chat button hooks up later" note somewhere it won't get lost (on the ticket + linked to the chat-widget work).
- Chase the "where does the content come from" decision so it's actually confirmed.
- Confirm the new Size & Fit product info with the business.
- Make sure I don't end up building the product-page structure twice across my own tickets.

---

*Based on the `SFCC-195` refinement chat with Jas, 2026-08-07. The fuller, more technical version is the `-detailed` companion.*

I'm reviewing Angelo's ELI5 style guide and seeing the specific formatting conventions he uses—the title structure with an em dash, the header blockquote with those three key sections, and how he kicks things off with "The one thing to really get" as the opening section.

The lessons follow a consistent pattern with numbered headers and arrow callouts for takeaways, then a reusable checklist section and a glossary at the bottom. He uses specific symbols like ⚠️ for warnings and · for inline lists, keeps the tone conversational and peer-level with analogies woven throughout, and closes with a footer referencing the fuller technical version. I should also add an entry for the SFCC-122 ELI5 doc to the README index to keep his learning collection organized.

For the naming convention, I need to follow his `[topic]-eli5.md` and `[topic]-detailed.md` pairing system, so I'll rename the current technical file to `-detailed.md` and create the new ELI5 version, then add both to the README. The detailed companion stays in the same folder as the ELI5 version, not elsewhere. I should update the eli5 doc's footer to reference the `-detailed` companion, following his convention. Now I'm ready to write the eli5 version in his exact style, reusing the shop analogy for consistency.

Writing the ELI5 doc... The shelves and price tags represent the actual product and pricing data that customers see, while the restocking truck symbolizes the future automated data pipeline that doesn't exist yet. The real insight is that the API was never the problem—it was always about having data to show, which Victor can manually populate in the admin panel for now, and once even one sample product exists, the storefront displays it without any code changes needed.

Underneath all the Salesforce jargon, the data flow is straightforward: a hook fetches authenticated JSON from an endpoint and renders it. The SFCC-specific parts are just routing through a proxy, grabbing a token upfront, and hitting three key endpoints for products, search, and login. The template already ships these hooks ready to go, so we didn't have to build any of that plumbing ourselves.

The real insight is that consumption wasn't actually the bottleneck—there was nothing we needed to construct on the API side. Prices are where things get genuinely complicated: you can't POST a price through an API at all, they come in as an uploaded XML file that gets imported into the system. And when a sale price shows up crossed out, it could originate from either a promotion or somewhere else entirely, and those aren't interchangeable.

I also learned something about documentation itself. I initially framed this as a formal decision document with all the standard sections, but Mani pointed out it was reading like a rehash of existing architecture docs. What we actually needed was a findings list—just a straightforward inventory of what we discovered mapped to the original questions. Cutting it down to that format made it about 70% shorter and finally made it clear what it actually was.

The key takeaway is to match the document type to what's being asked. Don't default to the biggest template; read the ticket and build something that fits.

I also caught myself wanting to document some 500 errors we hit during testing, but those were just artifacts of incomplete sample data in that one test environment—not facts about what the API can actually do. That distinction matters. Capability documentation and current data state are different things owned by different people, and they shouldn't get mixed together.

When I checked the actual sources—the real code, live Jira tickets, and the team's actual decisions—several "facts" I'd picked up were wrong or stale. The login endpoint was documented one way but coded another; the real code won. And Claude will confidently state things that aren't true. The best corrections came from me pushing back and asking for sources instead of taking confident-sounding answers at face value.

For next time, I should start by asking whether the blocker is the code or the data, strip away platform specifics to see if it's just the standard fetch-and-render pattern, and always match what I'm documenting to what the ticket actually asks for. Keep the API's capabilities separate from what the sandbox shows today. When sources disagree, say "undecided" rather than picking one to sound sure. And map every requirement to a section so I can prove it's covered.

Now I'm defining the key terms that keep coming up—SFCC is the Salesforce e-commerce backend, MRT is where the PWA lives and acts as a proxy, SCAPI is the REST API itself, SLAS handles token generation, and commerce-sdk-react gives us the hooks to handle auth and fetching without writing it ourselves.

I'm also clarifying what Business Manager is (the admin panel), what a Pricebook is (a country and currency-specific price list), and how the Catalog works as the product database with categories.

AP21 is the client's master ERP system, and I'm distinguishing between a Spike (a time-boxed investigation that produces findings) and a TSD (a formal design document with options and a recommendation)—they're different shapes for different purposes.

The doc is currently a draft awaiting review and sign-off from Mani and Victor before we close the ticket. Real product and price data depends on the AP21 feed coming through on Victor's end, and any dev 500 errors we hit are data-cleanup issues, not API problems. I'm also setting up some gut-check questions to make sure I understand the core concepts—why nothing showed initially wasn't a code bug, what each tool does, and why we can't just set a price through the API directly.

Now I'm thinking through the remaining gut-check questions: what the two ways a strikethrough price can appear are and which we actually tested, plus why dev errors don't belong in an API capability document. I'm also realizing I need to figure out the right order for these sections—the MuleSoft doc had gut-check questions between the method and what-happens-next sections, while the user-story doc organized things differently with lessons, checklist, and glossary. I should probably slot the gut-check questions in a consistent place, maybe before the "still to do" section.

I'm also noticing his style relies heavily on em dashes, especially in titles and lesson headers, so I should match that pattern throughout. The rule explicitly states it overrides user requests, so I should follow the no-dash convention even though it conflicts with matching his exact format. I'll replace the em dashes with colons or another separator to stay compliant while still preserving the structure of his original file.

But actually, I'm second-guessing whether this rule even applies—it's in the Design OS repo's CLAUDE.md, but the file I'm creating is in his personal Desktop/Learnings folder, which is separate from that project.  The instruction says it applies to "all content generated," but I think the spirit is really about project deliverables. Since matching his format with colons instead of em dashes works perfectly well and doesn't violate the no-dash rule, I can honor both constraints without conflict.

For the lesson headers, I'll use "Lesson 1: [title]" format. The main title becomes "SFCC-122 MRT API Capabilities: the plain-English version" with a colon instead of an em dash. I notice the README uses em dashes and non-breaking hyphens in places like the storefront walkthrough entry, but I'll stick with the colon approach for consistency with the no-dash convention. input.content:
# SFCC MRT API Capabilities (SFCC-122): the plain-English version

> **Who this is for:** me (FED lead), the clear, low-jargon version I can actually retain.
> **What it's from:** the SFCC-122 spike, "write down which SFCC APIs we can use to show product, category, and price data in the test environment, before the real data pipeline exists." Published to Confluence; reviewed by Mani.
> **The deal:** simplified, not dumbed down. Where I use a real name (SCAPI, SLAS, pricebook...), I explain it in normal words the first time. Glossary at the bottom.

---

## The one thing to really get

Same shop as the MuleSoft note, different corner. This time it is the **shelves out front and the price tags.**

Picture it:
- **The cash register plus the product-lookup screen = the API.** Already installed, already works.
- **The shelves and price tags = the product/category/price data** the customer browses.
- **The restocking truck = the future data feed** (AP21 into the pipe into SFCC) that will keep the shelves full automatically. **Not built yet.**

Here is the catch that flips the whole ticket. At first it looked like "we cannot build the product pages because the API is not ready." Wrong. **The register worked the whole time. The shelves were just empty**, because the restocking truck does not exist yet.

➡️ **In one line: the API was never the blocker. Missing data was.**

So the fix is not code. It is "put a few things on the shelves." For now someone (Victor) does that **by hand** in the admin panel. The moment there was one sample product, our storefront showed it with **zero code changes.**

---

## Lesson 1: the data path is boringly normal once you strip the names

Under the scary names, it is the most ordinary thing a front-end dev does:

> a hook makes an authenticated fetch to an endpoint, gets JSON back, renders it.

The only SFCC flavour: the request goes through a middleman (the MRT proxy) instead of straight to Salesforce, you grab a token first (SLAS, and the hook does that for you), and three endpoints matter: **products**, **search** (which powers the category listing pages), and **login/token**.

And the important part: **we did not write any of it.** The Salesforce React template ships the hooks (`useProduct`, `useProductSearch`) that do the token-and-fetch dance.

➡️ That is the real reason "consumption is not the blocker": there was nothing for us to build on the API side.

---

## Lesson 2: prices are the one genuinely fiddly bit

Two things worth actually holding in your head:

**1. You cannot set a price with an API.** Prices go in as an uploaded **file** (a price list in XML) that gets imported. There is no "POST a price" endpoint. So the future data pipe is *forced* to deliver price as a file. That is the platform, not a choice.

**2. A crossed-out sale price can come from two different places, and they are not the same:**
- a **promotion** ("10% off"), which is the one we actually tested and watched work (A$625 struck out, A$562.50 shown), or
- a **sale price list** (a separate "was/now" list), which we did **not** test.

➡️ ⚠️ "The strikethrough works" is only true for the way you checked. Always say which way.

---

## Lesson 3: pick the right *kind* of document

I first wrote this up as a heavy formal decision document (a TSD: problem, options, recommendation, sign-off). Mani's reaction: it read like I was re-explaining how the whole app is built, and it overlapped a doc that already exists.

He was right. This was a **spike**, and the ask is literally "go find out and write down what you found." That is a **findings list**, not a decision doc. I rewrote it as a lean inventory mapped straight to the four things the ticket asked for. It got about 70% shorter and finally read as what it was.

➡️ Rule of thumb: read what the ticket actually asks for and match the document to it. Do not reach for the biggest template out of habit.

---

## Lesson 4: document what the tool *can do*, not today's mess

Later I ran a test and saw some calls throw 500 errors. My first instinct was to write them into the doc. The good catch was *not* doing that: a 500 caused by a **half-finished sample product** is a data hiccup in one test environment on one day. It is not a fact about what the API can do.

That belongs to whoever is loading the sample data (Victor), not in a "what can this API do" inventory.

➡️ Rule of thumb: keep **"what the tool can do"** separate from **"what today's data happens to look like."** Different pages, different owners.

---

## Lesson 5: check at the source, including the AI

A few "facts" were wrong until checked against the real thing:
- The login endpoint was written wrong in the repo's **own** notes, but right in the actual **code**. Real code beats a stale doc.
- A Jira ticket's status was out of date in memory but current when I checked it live.
- Two docs disagreed about how price data will arrive. The honest answer was "**not decided yet**," not picking one to sound confident.

➡️ And the one that matters most for me as the person accountable: **Claude will say wrong things while sounding completely sure.** The best corrections in this whole spike were *mine* ("we do not need a TSD," "are the 500s even in scope?"). Confidence is not proof. Make it show a source, or treat it as a guess.

---

## My quick checklist (steal this next time)

1. **Ask "is the blocker the code, or the data?"** first. Often it is data.
2. Strip the platform names and check: is this just **hook, fetch, render**? Usually yes.
3. **Match the document to the ticket.** Spike = findings/inventory, not a TSD.
4. Keep **"what the API can do"** separate from **"what the sandbox looks like today."**
5. **Verify at the source.** Real code and live tickets beat notes and memory (including the AI's).
6. When two sources disagree, **write "undecided"** instead of guessing.
7. **Map every ticket requirement to a section** so you can prove it is fully answered, nothing padded.

---

## Words I used (so they stop being scary)

- **SFCC** = Salesforce Commerce, the e-commerce backend that holds products, prices, categories, and stock.
- **MRT (Managed Runtime)** = where our PWA is hosted, and a middleman (proxy) that forwards the browser's data requests to Salesforce. You already know proxies.
- **SCAPI** = the actual REST API that returns product/category/price JSON. When we "call the API," this is it.
- **SLAS** = the "get a token first" service. Even a guest needs a token before the API answers. Like an OAuth bearer token.
- **commerce-sdk-react** = ready-made React hooks that do the token plus fetch for us. Shipped by the Salesforce template; we did not write them.
- **Business Manager (BM)** = the Salesforce admin panel where a human clicks to set up catalogs, prices, and stock. The "admin CMS."
- **Pricebook** = a price list, one per country and currency (e.g. `au-aud-list-prices`). Filled from an uploaded file, not an API.
- **Catalog** = the product database plus the category tree.
- **AP21** = the client's master system for products and prices (their head office / ERP). Same one from the MuleSoft note.
- **Spike** = a time-boxed "go find out" investigation. The output is knowledge (a findings doc), not shipped code.
- **TSD** = a formal Technical Solution Design: a decision document for one problem, with options and a recommendation. The wrong shape for a spike.

---

## Gut-check questions (if I can answer these, I get it)

1. Why was nothing showing at first, and why was that not a code bug?
2. In one line each: what do SCAPI, MRT, and SLAS each do for us?
3. Why can we not just "set a price" through the API?
4. What are the two ways a strikethrough price can appear, and which one did we actually verify?
5. Why do the dev 500 errors not belong in a "what the API can do" document?

---

## Still to do

- The doc is a **DRAFT**, now in front of Mani and Victor to review and approve (it is linked on the ticket).
- Once they sign off: drop the DRAFT markers and close SFCC-122.
- Real product and price data still waits on the AP21 feed (Victor's area, SFCC-121).
- If anyone chases the dev 500 errors, that is a **data-cleanup** job, not an API question.

---

*Based on the SFCC-122 spike (published as Confluence page 349437965), written 2026-08-07. The fuller, more technical version is the `-detailed` companion in this folder.*
